⍞ Materials: Mapping the World with Art, notebook

NOTE: Ideally, you should have a notebook that is at least 8 x 10 inches, so you have room to draw your own maps and also glue in maps that are printed off.

➜ INTRO
This year, we are learning about mapmaking and global exploration. You will be learning to draw your own maps as well. You may want to first practice outlining the map on a whiteboard or another piece of paper before putting it in your notebook. As time permits on drawing days, you are encouraged to use watercolors or colored pencils to fill in your outlines (see the link for examples done by students). Your Geography notebook will be used on both days of the week. Make sure you label each entry with the date or lesson number. There will be days when you will be prompted to follow the instructions for an activity in the Activity Section of your Mapping the World with Art book.
∞ Image Link: Watercolor Map Examples

➜ READ
Reading 1: The Very Earliest Maps

➜ NARRATE & NOTEBOOK
1\. Narrate orally what you remember about the reading.
2\. Then, in your notebook, include some kind of narration. You can look back at the text as needed. You can write a short paragraph, write bullet points, or draw a concept map or pictures with captions. You can be as creative as you like. We provided examples of other students' work. Typically, each two-page spread in your notebook will have a narration on one side and your map drawings on the other. There may be weeks in which you will have two drawings per two-page spread (especially in Term 3).

⍞ Materials: Local Geography, notebook
Local Map

PREP: This lesson requires that you take a look at a local map of your area. There are some city or town websites that might have online versions of maps for you to view. However, if it is not easily found, Google Maps is an alternative source to use.

➜ MAP QUESTIONS
⍞ Map Resource: Local Map (suggest you use Google Maps)
1. Locate your street. (A parent will probably need to help.) Do you live within the city limits? Mark your street on the map.
2. Do you have a downtown or city center? If so, in what direction would you travel from your home to get there? Locate your local seat of government—city hall, town hall, or municipal building. Do you live north, south, east, or west of it?
3. How are the streets laid out in your city? Is any portion of your city laid out in a grid? (Older areas may utilize the grid. Newer sections may utilize cul-de-sacs. Other patterns like loop roads and diagonals may be used.) If so, what direction do the streets run? (north-south, east-west, etc.)
4. What are the streets named in this area? Do you see any “streets,” “avenues,” or “lanes”? What other street types (e.g., way, court, parkway) can you find? Is there a pattern for when these names are used (such as cul-de-sacs being “courts”)?
5. Locate your local police department, fire station, and hospital. How would you travel there from your home? Do you have more than one police station, fire station, or hospital? If so, mark where they are all located. Are they close to each other or far apart? What do you notice about how they are spaced?
6. Look for familiar places (grocery stores you go to, places of worship, friends' homes, etc.). How would you travel there from your home? Choose one of the familiar places you found and find at least 2 different routes to travel there from your home. Which one do you think is faster? Mark the familiar places on your map.
7. Locate any parks or outdoor areas in your city. Mark them on your map. What direction would you travel to get there? Are there any within walking distance from your home?

➜ INTRODUCTION
1\. In this term, we will follow the life of the naturalist John James Audubon as he explores the wilderness of America during the late 1800s, a time when the new frontier still had much to learn about the land’s wildlife.

The island of Haiti has two main languages: Haitian Creole and French. Due to its history of French colonization, the island still speaks and uses French in formal settings. The majority of people, however, speak Haitian Creole (French-influenced).
